title: Crystallised ginger
subtitle: fresh ginger slices cooked in sugar syrup, then dried in a sugar coating
excerpt: Crystallised ginger is fresh ginger slices simmered first in water to draw out some heat, then cooked in a concentrated sugar syrup until the slices turn translucent and absorb the sugar. The ginger is drained, rolled in caster sugar, and left to dry on a rack for several hours until the coating is firm and slightly gritty. It keeps for months in an airtight tin.
sourceNotes: Crystallised ginger documented in British confectionery and baking sources from at least the eighteenth century. The method of parboiling first to reduce pungency before candying in syrup is standard in British and American confectionery manuals.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of saturating a fruit or vegetable with sugar syrup by repeated soaking or simmering, until the water in the food is replaced with sugar. The result preserves the ingredient and gives a sweet, translucent finish.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 3 months.

content.text: Crystallised ginger is fresh ginger slices that have been

in sugar syrup until translucent, then rolled in caster sugar and dried until the coating sets. The ginger is parboiled first to soften it and draw out some of the sharpest heat. The result is intensely spiced, sweet, and chewy, with a firm sugary crust.

items.prepNote: divided: 300 g for syrup, 100 g for coating

content.text: Put the sliced ginger into a saucepan and cover generously with cold water. Bring to the boil, then drain. Repeat once more: boil, drain. The double parboil reduces the fieriness without removing all the flavour.
Put 300 g caster sugar and 400 ml water into the saucepan and stir over a low heat until the sugar dissolves. Add the drained ginger slices.

Simmer on a low heat for 40 to 45 minutes, stirring now and then. The ginger is ready when each slice looks translucent and the syrup is thick and sticky. Check the pan often in the last 10 minutes. The syrup can burn once most of the water has gone.
Remove from the heat. Lift the ginger pieces out with a fork or slotted spoon and place them in a single layer on a cooling rack set over a tray to catch the drips.
While still warm and tacky, toss the ginger slices in the remaining 100 g caster sugar. Make sure each slice is well coated on both sides.
Spread the pieces back onto the rack in a single layer. Leave to dry at room temperature for 4 to 6 hours. The sugar coating should feel dry and slightly gritty, not sticky, when ready.

attrs.problem: Syrup crystallised and turned grainy in the pan
attrs.avoid: Avoid stirring the syrup during the reduction once the sugar has dissolved; movement encourages crystallisation.
attrs.fix: If the syrup crystallises, add a splash of water and warm gently over a low heat without stirring until the crystals dissolve again.

attrs.problem: Ginger slices still tough after cooking
attrs.avoid: Avoid under-cooking; ginger needs the full simmering time to soften.
attrs.fix: Continue simmering for another 10 to 15 minutes, checking for tenderness with a fork. Young ginger softens faster than old ginger.

attrs.problem: Sugar coating sticky and not drying
attrs.avoid: Avoid coating in too thick a layer of sugar; it traps moisture and stays tacky.
attrs.fix: Shake off excess sugar before drying and leave in a warm, dry room. A very gentle oven on its lowest setting for 20 minutes speeds the process.
